fragments.gist: Frontmatter: skill name and trigger description (layered creation and legacy migration of global_spec.json per SPEC_STANDARD.md).
Purpose: the skill covers the path from idea to a complete global_spec.json before the factory, does not replace factory validation, and names SPEC_STANDARD.md as normative.
Core problem: a top-down LLM-written spec can be structurally valid yet semantically hollow - the 'placeholder problem'.
Defines a placeholder and lists examples: dict->dict signatures, generic Result DTOs, manager/utils modules, vague MUST notes, functions implementable as return [] / {} / None.
Placeholders must be prevented during authoring rather than reported after the full spec is written.
Working mode: semi-manual with the user, never a full spec from a short idea; per layer discuss, record, list open questions, test for placeholders, proceed when stable; going back is normal.
For large cases use tools/design_index.py, which has a structural view (items, explicit A*/OQ-* references) and a lexical view (name occurrences with context).
A lexical --mentions occurrence is never architectural evidence; do not infer ownership, clusters or relations from it.
fragments.proposed_question: Is every ownership or relation claim backed by a normative source you read, not by a shared name or --mentions hit?

fragments.gist: Each addressable decision is one heading with all owned content under strictly deeper headings; '## Accepted decision' without ID gets a source:* key; a same-or-shallower heading closes the item.

Every normative State 2 document must contain at least one indexed accepted-decision item, otherwise it is invisible to design_lint (no per-file gate read; only the case-level missing_security_review check implies one indexed decision).
Repeated section titles must be qualified so ITEM + SECTION stays unique; extra headings are legal and must not be flattened.

State 2 decisions carry Normative rules, Formal invariant(s), Required tests, Consequence; the text calls a missing one a 'review prompt', which contradicts the fence that raises that warning to a stop.
Command list for design_index.py (--list, --get, --references, --mentions, --context) and design_lint.py; prefer them over raw grep; source Markdown stays normative.
For legacy migration read LEGACY_MIGRATION_EVIDENCE.md before touching any design-state artifact or global_spec.json; do not start from notes or a target schema.
Probe output is evidence only; classify each finding as derivable, product value, backend lowering, irregular responsibility or unresolved; unresolved is BLOCK and code frequency never resolves it.

Primary rule: never design the next layer over decisions hidden by generic names/types/prose; if contracts invent models go back to models, if notes invent behaviour go back to rules, if a module needs utils go back to responsibilities.
The fence: no warnings, no waivers; every tool passes findings through tools/fence.py, which raises warning/review to a stop and attaches a 'not decided - decide: ...' hint.
closure_gap_waivers.json is not permission: its presence blocks Stage 9 until every waived gap is a recorded decision with an owner carried by a contract.
Module review result is PASS or AMBIGUITY only; PASS_INTERNAL_VARIATION was removed because a mechanism that may vary is undecided.
Assembly runs two extra checks: witness (each decision with formal invariants names a verified witness) and flows (each State 4 capability is planned, contracted and reached from a route).
A dirty Workbench or Factory checkout blocks admission and no flag softens it; author rule: not decided -> decide.

The frontier: `tools/obligations <case> next|focus` rebuilds a typed obligation graph each run (defining blocks dependents, convergence does not; LOCAL/SYSTEM axes); use it to pick which obligation to close; see tools/OBLIGATIONS.md.
Design states are ordered by dependency, not by the section order of global_spec.json.
State 0 capture list: goal, actors, primary actions, inputs, observable outputs, persistent data, external systems, constraints, explicit open questions.
State 0 must not contain Python contracts, helper functions, module paths, algorithms or speculative extension points.
State 0 readiness: value stated in one concrete paragraph, each action paired with an observable outcome, failure outcomes known, unknowns written as unknowns.
fragments.proposed_question: Does every primary action have an observable outcome and known failure outcome, with unknowns written as open questions rather than abstractions?

fragments.gist: Record trust boundaries at State 0 via the mandatory route in SECURITY_REVIEW_EVIDENCE.md; do not defer unknown actors, ingress, credentials or external trust to module design.
State 1: start from domain meaning; per model decide why it exists, its role, creator, readers, modifiers, persistence, lifecycle, source of every required field, partial construction, invariants.
fragments.proposed_question: For each model: why does it exist, who creates, reads and modifies it, and where does every required field come from?

fragments.gist: Reject model placeholders (data: dict, metadata: dict, payload: Any, status: str, result: object, extra: dict) unless an external contract is explicitly required to be open-ended.
Every runtime model closes identity as value or entity; undetermined means BLOCK and no entry into State 2; procedure in MODEL_IDENTITY_EVIDENCE.md.
Record security-relevant entity semantics at State 1 via the State 1 route of SECURITY_REVIEW_EVIDENCE.md without redefining identity.

State 1 readiness: every required field has a producer, models explainable without helper functions, behaviour-relevant states explicit, concepts separated by reason to change, no 'for flexibility' fields.
fragments.proposed_question: Is every field needed by a stated requirement, and are concepts that change for different reasons kept as separate models?

fragments.gist: State 1 output is draft models, candidate constants/catalogs and open model questions; contracts are not finalized yet.

State 2: separate always-true statements from runtime-configuring values; capture invariants, access rules, transitions, policies, thresholds, fallbacks, knobs, limits/paths/timeouts, stable catalogs. Says nothing about where values live beyond the four section names below.
fragments.proposed_question: Which statements must always hold, and which values merely configure behaviour; is each recorded as an accepted decision?

fragments.gist: A value describing an external system keeps its ordinary config/models/rules home but must be bound to a content-addressed Workbench evidence record (EXTERNAL_CONTRACT_EVIDENCE.md); typed-but-unsourced is not closed.
Before State 3 complete the mandatory security gate: every required category has an explicit outcome and any UNRESOLVED is BLOCK.

Data placement as the skill tells it: config = independently changing runtime/product knobs, rules = read-only domain/policy semantics, models = schemas/taxonomies/structured catalogs, notes = behaviour that uses the data, not the data. It gives a thematic four-way split only - no ordered placement procedure, and nothing on how values reach generated code (addresses, deterministic data emitter, model never sees values).
State 2 navigation recipe: --list decisions, --get/--references before changing one, --mentions for shared names, --context for a hit; do not turn shared names into ownership links.
State 2 readiness (first half): every invariant is owned by a future responsibility, not 'the whole system'; state transitions explicit where lifecycle matters.
fragments.proposed_question: Does each invariant name one future owning responsibility, and is every lifecycle-relevant state transition written explicitly?

fragments.gist: State 2 readiness (second half): tables and allow-lists are stored outside notes, and a value's section is justified by why and how it changes - the only hint at the standard's operational placement test.
State 3: derive modules from ownership of complexity, rules and knowledge, not from screens, endpoints or verbs.
fragments.proposed_question: Is each module justified by the knowledge and rules it owns rather than by a screen, endpoint or verb?

fragments.gist: Bridge from State 2: treat the decision index as evidence inventory; per candidate run --get, --references, --mentions, --context and assign one primary enforcement owner only after reading the source; the index never generates module names.
Per module define responsibility, owned knowledge, decisions, hidden details, public capabilities, what it must not own, allowed dependencies, expected consumers.
Prefer deep modules: narrow public API, substantial hidden responsibility, stable ownership boundary, no leaked internal sequencing.

Cohesion test: a module is deep only if most public capabilities rest on one hidden mechanism, one invariant set, one reason to change; a shared entity or product word is taxonomy, and a domain area maps to several deep modules plus an optional thin facade.
fragments.proposed_question: Do most public capabilities of this module rest on one hidden mechanism with one reason to change, or only share an entity name?

fragments.gist: Every module records a machine-read '### Depth assessment' (kind: deep + hidden mechanism, or kind: facade + delegates to); missing declaration is a State 3 error for wide (>= WIDE_SURFACE_CAPABILITIES) and narrow modules alike.

Split triggers (judgement part): several independent state machines, unrelated transactional topologies, near-disjoint dependency sets, per-operation large algorithms, consumers needing only an API subset.
fragments.proposed_question: Does the candidate hold several state machines, transaction topologies, disjoint dependency sets or consumer subsets that mean it is several modules?

fragments.gist: Split trigger (mechanical part): public surface nearly equals the whole owned function surface (State 6 reports module_surface_not_deep); plus the start of the 'change in one rule group' trigger that continues past line 470.
Tail of the split-trigger list plus the per-operation probe: shared mechanism, shared invariants, same reason to change, same dependencies, subset consumers; split along mechanism, never size.
fragments.proposed_question: Do this module's public operations share one mechanism, invariants, dependencies and reason to change, or does it split along the mechanism?

fragments.gist: A thin facade is admissible only when declared `kind: facade`, owns no policy and delegates to deep modules; undeclared shallowness is collapse.
Warning sign: generic module names (utils, helpers, common, manager, processor, service) without a domain qualifier; the gate matches exact names only, not the 'without qualifier' nuance.

Warning signs: router/API owning policy, storage deciding semantics, rendering mutating state, forwarding-only modules, one module per endpoint or per entity, public API equal to internals (last one is reported by State 6 module_surface_not_deep).
fragments.proposed_question: Does any module own policy outside its role, merely forward arguments, or mirror an endpoint or entity instead of a mechanism?

fragments.gist: Readiness: every invariant has one primary enforcement owner and every model's creation/mutation has a responsible module; the 2->3 trace gate covers the decision/invariant half, model creation ownership was not seen gated here.
Readiness: each module hides something meaningful and names that one mechanism in its Depth assessment.
Readiness: public API smaller than internal behaviour; would any split trigger fire if the module were one file.
fragments.proposed_question: Is the public API smaller than the hidden behaviour, and would any split trigger fire if this module were one file?

fragments.gist: Readiness: forbidden responsibilities are explicit (the 'Must not own' section is a required State 3 section).

Expected State 3 output described as draft global_spec sections (module_functions, imports.internal, module_order, module_paths); describes which artifact to produce and predates the markdown State 3 artifact the gate reads.

State 4: walk a few end-to-end flows using the trigger -> boundary -> policy -> domain operation -> storage -> observable result template; the gate requires Trigger, Boundary, Steps, Outcomes, Errors sections per flow.
At every flow transition determine crossing model, next decision owner, adapter need, possible errors, error translator, produced state/artifact, cleanup or rollback.
fragments.proposed_question: At each flow transition, are the crossing model, next decision owner, adapter, error translator and cleanup duty named?

fragments.gist: Flows are not a test-case enumeration; their purpose is to expose missing ownership, missing data and broken boundaries.
State 4 readiness: flows end in observable result or explicit failure, a module produces each result, error boundaries owned, adapters visible, no hidden business logic in endpoints.
fragments.proposed_question: Does every major flow end in an observable result or explicit failure produced by a named module, with no logic hidden in endpoints?

fragments.gist: State 5: define only cross-module operations; each needs owner, callers, inputs, outputs, observable effect, enforced policy, errors, state impact - exactly the gate's required sections.

Do not expose internal algorithm steps; readiness: real cross-module need, callers ignorant of sequencing, removal would break ownership, outputs concrete (flow lineage of each public op is gated, the rest is judgement).
fragments.proposed_question: Does each public operation serve a real cross-module need, hide internal sequencing, and return an output concrete enough to forbid empty results?

fragments.gist: Expected State 5 output: stable imports.internal and top-level module_functions entries plus dependency-boundary decisions to lower into implementation_obligations.
State 6 opens: create exact typed Python signatures.
If the project uses deterministic HTTP assembly read ROUTER_IR_GUIDE.md after contracts stabilise and build rules.http_router_backend from accepted flows; never derive signatures from route rows.
Use real project types; for every public operation create the exact contract, plan internal functions, give every public and private function a contract, set function_order.
Chain product operation -> capability -> deep module -> facade; a module whose functions are almost all public is reported as module_surface_not_deep and must be fixed in State 3, not State 6.

Every interface used as a dependency parameter needs a structural local/external decision in implementation_obligations; a local class must contract the full interface surface, __init__ alone is not enough.

State 6 lint reports interface_without_provider when a function returns an interface no planned class implements, with prescription entries; do not infer the relation from class names or a composition note.
Do not introduce new domain concepts silently in State 6; an undefined type, ambiguous result or new state sends the author back to an earlier state.

Reject generic contract placeholders (dict -> dict, Any -> Any, object, Mapping[str, Any]) unless generic openness is an explicit external contract; only the experimental advisory lint checks it, it is not in the phase sequence.

State 6 readiness: every argument has a source, every return a consumer, each function one owning module, public/private distinguishable by API ownership (value-flow coverage tool addresses part of this; check not read).
fragments.proposed_question: Does every argument have a clear source, every return value a consumer, and every function exactly one owning module?

fragments.gist: State 6 readiness: every interface-typed dependency has a local/external disposition and each local class covers every port method.
State 7: write notes only after contracts and ownership are stable; notes specify behaviour not in the signature; use the closed note class registry of the standard.

Per-function checklist that paraphrases the note class registry; its only word on data reference is the bare item 'rule, model, or config references' - no `= rules.*` / `= config.*` syntax, nothing on constants or imported symbols.
Avoid restating the function name, repeating the signature, implementation pseudocode and inline policy tables (the only hint that data must not be inlined in notes; no address form is given).
Avoid vague adjectives (properly, correctly, appropriately, as needed) and requirements that cannot tell a real implementation from a stub.
Placeholder resistance test: could the contract be satisfied by return None/[]/{}, an empty model, constant success or plain forwarding; if so strengthen an earlier layer or drop the function.
fragments.proposed_question: Could this function be implemented as return None, an empty value, a constant or plain forwarding without contradicting its notes?

fragments.gist: State 7 readiness: observable outcome explicit, output fields assigned or projected from known sources, invalid inputs and external failures defined, side effects and forbidden shortcuts explicit.
fragments.proposed_question: Are this function's observable outcome, output field sources, failure behaviour, side effects and forbidden shortcuts all stated in its notes?

fragments.gist: Sole data-reference requirement of State 7: 'Do notes refer addressably to config, models, and rules?' - it never shows the `= config.*` / `= models.*` / `= rules.*` form, never mentions constants, imported symbols, smallest-node addressing, leaf reachability or the no-literal rule.
State 8: assemble global_spec.json with all standard sections; the list omits standard_version, persistence, properties, determinism and names module_hints, which the standard does not define.
Third-party and stdlib imports of an owned module go into imports.third_party_by_module / imports.stdlib_by_module, not prose.
Assembly only serialises decisions already made and is not a creative pass; missing models, unclear ownership or vague behaviour send the author back to an earlier state.
After assembly use the existing factory validators and inspectors instead of duplicating them in the skill.
Run the Workbench external-contract check before module review; an active verified binding changed without reciprocal supersession is a BLOCK and its fingerprint is never refreshed automatically.
Stage 8.1: review every assembled module slice; zero structural blocks is not a semantic verdict; record classification and slice hash, and a review goes stale when the hash changes.
Stage 9 is operational: run the read-only admission gate (design_factory_admission.py <case> --project ... --update-existing) against the target Factory checkout before copying anything.

Proceed only from READY_TO_EXPORT: clean committed source, closed current 8.1 review, ready assembly, matching standards, Factory validator PASS, closed semantic-test handoff, explicit authorisation to replace a canonical target.
Use export_to_factory.py only after admission; export records source commit, hashes, tool fingerprints and validation evidence; Route B, deploy, verification and OTK belong to the Factory.
External-contract evidence is fingerprinted by Workbench admission; the Factory receives closed spec IR and is not an evidence authority.
Placeholder taxonomy heading: apply the taxonomy during every state.
Product placeholder: a broad promise ('manage documents') without observable result; replace with concrete actions, outputs, failures.
fragments.proposed_question: Does every product promise name a concrete user action, its observable output and its failure?

fragments.gist: Model placeholder: generic containers (data: dict, metadata: dict, result: Any, one universal status) standing in for undecided structure; experimental lint flags generic field types.
fragments.proposed_question: Is any dict, Any, metadata bag or shared status field standing in for a model structure not yet decided?

fragments.gist: Rule placeholder: policy written as prose but not decided ('best strategy', 'reasonable limits'); replace with a declared rule, config value, ordering or explicit open question.
fragments.proposed_question: Is every policy a declared rule, config value, ordering or recorded open question rather than prose like 'best' or 'reasonable'?

fragments.gist: Module placeholder: a name that collects behaviour without owning a responsibility (utils, helpers, manager, processor, common_service); exact generic names are already a State 3 error.
fragments.proposed_question: Does each module name state one ownership boundary, or does it only collect behaviour nobody else owns?

fragments.gist: Contract placeholder: signatures that preserve uncertainty (dict -> dict, Any -> Any, broad optional parameters for hypothetical reuse).
fragments.proposed_question: Does any signature keep uncertainty through dict, Any, object, or optional parameters added only for hypothetical reuse?

fragments.gist: Behavioral placeholder: normative-sounding notes that constrain nothing ('MUST handle errors', 'MUST return the result'); the notes gate blocks a fixed list of stub phrasings.
fragments.proposed_question: Does each MUST note name a specific condition, outcome, assignment or boundary that a stub implementation would violate?

fragments.gist: Orchestration placeholder: a call sequence exists but no component owns producing the promised state, artifact or result.
fragments.proposed_question: For every promised state, artifact or result in this flow, which single component produces it?

fragments.gist: Future placeholder: speculative extension points (plugin interfaces without a plugin, 'for future use' fields, undefined format branches, premature base classes); record future ideas outside the spec.
fragments.proposed_question: Is every interface, optional field and format branch required by a present product need rather than a future one?

fragments.gist: Interaction protocol steps: state current design state, summarise stable decisions, surface open questions, stay in the current state, show a compact draft, run resistance questions, move on; current state and next step are tool output.
Conversation manner: small coherent groups of questions, concrete proposals with a recommended trade-off, do not re-ask established facts.

Output discipline: use compact working artifacts (Model and Module card examples) in early states and convert to global_spec.json only later; the card format belongs to the state templates the gates parse.
Completion criteria: a recap of every state's readiness question plus external evidence coverage and standard conformance; operationally readiness is the admission verdict READY_TO_EXPORT.
Objective: not maximal detail, only enough precision that the factory need not invent architecture or product semantics.
